html:
The Khmer Empire was the great power of mainland Southeast Asia from 802 to 1431, centred on the city of Angkor in what is now northern Cambodia. At its height it ruled or held as vassals most of the mainland, from southern Vietnam to parts of Laos and Thailand.

Its start is dated to 802, when the prince Jayavarman II declared himself universal ruler on the Kulen hills, freeing the Khmer lands from Java's influence. The empire grew out of earlier Khmer states such as Chenla, which had taken over from Funan.

Angkor was a "hydraulic city": huge reservoirs, canals and moats stored monsoon water for rice fields across a wide plain. Surveys from the air show a low-density urban sprawl that made it one of the largest pre-industrial cities in the world. Its kings built a state temple each, and the best known came in two great reigns:

  • Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat, a Hindu temple to Vishnu, in the first half of the 12th century.
  • Jayavarman VII drove out the Cham who had sacked the city in 1177, then built the walled city of Angkor Thom and the Bayon, with its smiling stone faces, as a Buddhist king.

Wars with Champa and the Thai kingdoms ran through its history. The Chinese envoy Zhou Daguan left a lively account of the city in 1296 and 1297. Over the 14th century the empire shrank. Theravada Buddhism replaced the royal cults, Thai states grew stronger, and droughts and floods damaged the water system. The traditional end date is 1431, when Ayutthaya took Angkor; the court moved south toward Phnom Penh, and the old city was slowly abandoned except for its monasteries.
